title: Alegria illustration system for Facebook (Buck)
lede: The illustration and animation system that Buck designed for Facebook from 2017: flat figures built from circles and tubes, with long limbs and blue, violet, or pink skin.
summary: Buck’s flat, geometric figures for Facebook, with oversized limbs and non-natural skin. The core example of the style.
made: Commissioned 2017; Buck gives an end date of 8 February 2020 in its project data

evidence.note: Inspected three images from Buck’s project page at 1400 px wide: the cover image of the printed style guide (`alegria_thumbnail.png`), a hero illustration of figures carrying a thumbs-up, and a spread titled “Figure Construction”. None is stored.

styles.note: The reference work of the style: Buck’s own page describes “flat, minimal, geometric shapes” and figures with “oversized limbs and non-representational skin colors”.

context: Buck describes the project as “a new style guide, illustration and animation system for the entire Facebook ecosystem” and says Facebook engaged it in 2017. “Alegria is Spanish for ‘joy’.” [Buck](https://buck.co/work/facebook-alegria).

Buck credits Xoana Herrera as design lead, Amelia Giller and Janice Ahn as senior art directors, and ten core illustrators. The library also covers transport, plants, animals, buildings, and hands. [Buck](https://buck.co/work/facebook-alegria).

AIGA Eye on Design (21 August 2019) treats Alegria as the model for the tech illustration style and quotes Herrera on “ethnically non-specific” characters. [AIGA Eye on Design](https://eyeondesign.aiga.org/dont-worry-these-gangley-armed-cartoons-are-here-to-protect-you-from-big-tech/).
observed: In the hero illustration, six figures in flat fills carry a large blue thumbs-up. Arms and legs are long tubes that bend in smooth curves; one figure rides a unicycle.
Skin is violet, pink, pale blue, green, and yellow. Hair and some trousers are near-black navy.
Heads are small in relation to the bodies, and faces have only dots and short lines.
Some limbs carry a fine speckled grain in one tone, and a few details use thin colored lines.
A style-guide spread titled “Figure Construction” says the figures are “11 1/2 heads tall”, that “limbs are composed of cylindrical shapes”, and that men’s arms reach the knee.
Other guide pages show a woman with blue skin holding up a cup, a dog and fruit built from circles, and a rule on how to crop tall figures at the frame edge.
interpretation: The construction rules (heads as circles, limbs as cylinders, 11½ heads tall) explain why the style spread so fast: any illustrator can follow them and the results match.
The grain on some limbs shows that the original system allowed a little texture. Many later imitations removed it and kept only flat fills.
borrow: Build figures to a fixed head count (about 11 heads tall) with cylinder limbs, so a team of illustrators produces matching people.
Give each scene one oversized object that the figures lift or carry together.
